response.answer: Cyclododecane is used for fragile specimen preparation, minimizing surface removal to ≤50 µm, aligning with conservation policies. Alternative methods include laser ablation and epoxy impregnation. These methods ensure minimal artifact introduction.

Laser ablated specimens showed improvement in bond strength and predominantly cohesive failure mode in the adhesive as the pitch of the ablation pattern was reduced both before and after immersion in boiling water for 72 h. Based on the XPS and SLS results, parallel lines ablated at greater than 600 mW power and at less than 50.8 µm pitch resulted in roughened surfaces with increased titania and alumina content which, when bonded with the PETI-5 adhesive, formed robust bonds with apparent shear strengths comparable to current state-of-the-art surface preparation techniques [20].

results.title: Matthew Brown - The University of Texas at Austin
results.content: more Over the past decade, cyclododecane (CDD) has been increasingly adopted by vertebrate fossil preparators as a more e ective and advantageous material for several standard treatments and for new applications borrowed from art and artefact conservation. Many techniques in palaeontology utilise CDD's special properties, including its use as a temporary embedding and support material to protect fragile specimens during removal of rock matrix; as a barrier layer during consolidation; as a temporary consolidant; as a temporary ller during airscribe preparation; as acid-resistant protection for fossil bone during dissolution of the limestone matrix; as a gap-ller, sealant and separator during silicone rubber moulding; and as a protective coating for specimens that are otherwise too delicate to ship. In such cases, traditional methods of field jacket removal and fossil preparation can cause damage or destruction of the fossils within. Many techniques in palaeontology utilise CDD's special properties, including its use as a temporary embedding and support material to protect fragile specimens during removal of rock matrix; as a barrier layer during consolidation; as a temporary consolidant; as a temporary ller during airscribe preparation; as acid-resistant protection for fossil bone during dissolution of the limestone matrix; as a gap-ller, sealant and separator during silicone rubber moulding; and as a protective coating for specimens that are otherwise too delicate to ship. more The 2011 SVP Preparators Grant was awarded to Matthew Brown for the proposal titled "Teaching fossil preparation methods, developing standards and curricula" submitted by Brown, Amy Davidson, and Matt Smith. A group of Pive preparators participated in a six day writing workshop hosted at The University of Texas at Austin Vertebrate Paleontology Laboratory, tasked with the goal to "dePine standards for preparation and identify necessary skills and abilities required to competently prepare fossils." Two products were completed, a white paper outlining essential competencies for preparation, and a sample curriculum for teaching paleontological laboratory methods.
